summary: Explains how IP-based emergency calling mechanisms can support the next generation of the Pan-European in-vehicle eCall system, where cars place emergency calls with crash data. It also registers media types, an Emergency Call Data Type, and a SIP INFO package for carrying that data.

plainLanguage.summary: If a car crashes, it calls for help by itself and tells the helpers where it is. This describes how that call works on the modern internet.

questions: how do cars send emergency calls over ip
what is the minimum set of data in ecall
subtitle: How a crashed car can use ordinary IP emergency calling to send its location and vehicle data to the emergency call taker.

tldr.problem: Pan-European eCall lets vehicles place emergency calls that carry crash and location data, but the legacy system does this over circuit-switched GSM or UMTS calls using an in-band modem, which does not fit an all-IP network.
tldr.mechanism: The vehicle's in-vehicle system (IVS) places a SIP emergency call to a special eCall service URN and attaches its Minimum Set of Data (MSD) as a MIME body part. The emergency call center (PSAP) answers with an XML control block that acknowledges the data or asks for a fresh copy.
tldr.outcome: The RFC registers the service URNs, two MIME types, an INFO package and two registries, and is written generically so other regions can reuse it.

today: RFC 8147 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the IETF definition of NG-eCall signaling.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
eCall is a standardized and mandated system for emergency calls placed by vehicles, with a voice channel and a standard set of vehicle, sensor and location data. A call can be triggered automatically (a crash or other serious incident) or manually by an occupant. The call is routed to a specialized Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), where the data is available to the call taker.

Legacy eCall is a 3GPP circuit-switched call over GSM or UMTS, with an in-band modem carrying the data inside the voice channel. NG-eCall moves to all-IP. RFC 8147 describes how IETF mechanisms for IP-based emergency calls, including RFC 6443 and RFC 7852, provide the signaling and data exchange for it.

The scope is limited to the SIP framework. Cellular specifics, domain selection and call routing are left to other bodies, and migration between legacy and next-generation eCall is out of scope. The design is generic enough to be reused elsewhere, for example by RFC 8148.
sections.plainLanguage: A car that crashes can phone for help on its own. Old cars squeak their data through the voice line; this document makes the call work over the internet instead.

sections.title: The Vehicle Data (MSD)
sections.content:
Pan-European eCall defines a standard set of vehicle data called the Minimum Set of Data (MSD). It includes the VIN, vehicle type, propulsion type, current and optionally previous location, and the number of occupants. CEN specifies it in EN 15722, with both ASN.1 and XML encodings. Both circuit-switched eCall and this RFC use the ASN.1 PER encoding; the XML encoding is not used.

Because ASN.1 PER is binary, the MSD is sent with binary content transfer encoding inside SIP. The RFC registers the MIME type application/EmergencyCallData.eCall.MSD for it and adds eCall.MSD to the Emergency Call Data Types registry from RFC 7852.
sections.plainLanguage: The MSD is a small form the car fills in: which car it is, where it is, and how many people are inside.

sections.title: Carrying Data in SIP
sections.content:
The RFC reuses the RFC 7852 mechanism for data blocks in SIP emergency calls. The MSD or a control block travels as a MIME body part with its own Content-ID, always inside a multipart body. A top-level Call-Info header points to it with a cid: URL and a purpose value (EmergencyCallData.eCall.MSD or EmergencyCallData.Control). The body part has a Content-Disposition of By-Reference.

The IVS puts the MSD in the initial INVITE, optionally with a control block listing its capabilities. These parts use handling=optional, so a legacy element that does not understand them does not reject the call. The PSAP acknowledges the MSD with a control block in the final response (not in provisional ones such as 180). A PSAP can also decline a call but still say it got the MSD by sending received=true with a 600, 486 or 603 response.

Mid-call, the PSAP can ask for an updated MSD in a SIP INFO request, and the IVS replies with the MSD in a new INFO. If it cannot, it sends a control block with an actionResult of success=false and a reason. The IVS is not expected to send an unsolicited MSD after the initial INVITE. If the IVS gets a final response with no control block, the dialog is not an NG-eCall, for example because part of the path is legacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The car tucks its form into the first message it sends. The helper writes back 'got it', and later can say 'send it again, please'.

sections.title: Call Setup and Test Calls
sections.content:
A legacy eCall is a 112 call with an eCall flag. For NG-eCall, the IVS places an emergency call using a service URN that marks the call as an eCall and says whether it was triggered manually or automatically. The network recognizes the URN and routes the call to an NG-eCall-capable PSAP. The RFC adds two children under the sos subservice: urn:service:sos.ecall.automatic and urn:service:sos.ecall.manual. Call routing itself is out of scope.

eCall also needs test calls. These are recognized as eCalls to some extent but get no emergency treatment and reach no call taker. A service URN starting with test. marks such a call, and this RFC defines urn:service:test.sos.ecall for eCall. How a test call is handled is left to mobile operators, authorities and PSAPs.
sections.plainLanguage: The car dials a special address that says 'crash, automatic' or 'someone pressed the button'. There is also a practice address for checking that everything works.

sections.title: The Metadata/Control Block
sections.content:
The control block is an XML structure that works as a high-level protocol between PSAP and IVS. It uses the MIME type application/EmergencyCallData.Control+xml and has three elements:

  • ack acknowledges a data object or request. It has a mandatory ref (the Content-ID of the acknowledged part) and a received boolean that a PSAP must include. The PSAP MUST acknowledge an unsolicited MSD.
  • capabilities is optional and sent by the IVS, with one request child per supported action. Leaving it out means the IVS supports only send-data for eCall.MSD.
  • request is how the PSAP asks the vehicle to act. Its mandatory action attribute draws from an IANA registry, whose only initial value is send-data. A send-data request names a datatype, and only eCall.MSD must be supported.

The ack element can contain an actionResult with the action, a success flag, and, on failure, a reason and optional human-readable details. Several other attributes (int-id, persistence, supported-values, requested-state, element-id) exist only as extension points.
sections.plainLanguage: The control block is a short note passed back and forth: 'I got your form', 'please send it again', or 'sorry, I cannot, I am broken'.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The considerations of RFC 5069 and RFC 7852 apply. The MSD carries identifying and personal information, mostly about the vehicle and less about the owner, plus location, so it needs protection against unauthorized disclosure. Local regulations may add privacy requirements.

The IVS-supplied location in the MSD can be a useful sanity check against the network-provided location, but RFC 7378 discusses trust issues with device-provided location. An attacker able to answer the initial INVITE could send a 600, 486 or 603 response with a control block claiming received=true, making the IVS think the PSAP is overloaded and not retry. The risk can be mitigated as described in the IANA registration for the control media type, which also notes that control information should come only from a PSAP or other emergency provider and not be modified en route.

Data from outside sources can carry implementation risks such as buffer overflows or malformed XML, so implementations should follow best practices and expect malformed or oversized objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The car's form has private details, so it must not be shown to strangers. And a fake 'we got it' reply must not trick the car into giving up on calling.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC establishes a new EmergencyCallData media subtree under application, used only for emergency communications. It registers the service URNs from the call setup section, the MIME types for the MSD and the control block, the eCall.MSD and Control entries in the Emergency Call Data Types registry, and an XML namespace for the control block.

It also creates the Emergency Call Actions registry (initial value send-data) and the Emergency Call Action Failure Reasons registry, both under Expert Review. Finally it registers the EmergencyCallData.eCall.MSD SIP INFO package, which both endpoints list in a Recv-Info header to show they can receive INFO requests carrying this data.
